candidato.titulo: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
candidato.resumo: Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.

texto_fonte:
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Friday, October 23, 2026
A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
Experimental drug invika halts progression of refractory tumors by selectively stimulating tumor-fighting T cells.
Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the pioneering treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy. A study led by researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Mass General Brigham and Memorial Sloan Kettering found that, at optimal doses, invika was well tolerated and, in patients whose solid tumors had resisted standard immunotherapy, halted disease progression in most and shrank tumors in some.
“Patients whose tumors are advanced — particularly tumors that don’t respond well to immunotherapy — often have their backs against a wall. Few options remain once you reach that point, but these results highlight a more precise means of stimulating anti-tumor immunity that could provide another solution,” said co-corresponding author James Gulley, M.D., Ph.D., clinical director at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR), part of NIH’s National Cancer Institute (NCI).
While immunotherapies have already transformed treatment for several cancers, many patients benefit from them for only a short time, or not at all. Tumors frequently adapt to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies, such as pembrolizumab, limiting long-term benefits. Other strategies aim to rally T cells, the frontline soldiers of adaptive immunity, but usually do so indiscriminately, commonly leading to severe side effects.
Scientists designed the protein invika to engage a small subset of T cells, two groups of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes specifically. By activating only this narrow population rather than T cells broadly, invika is designed to drive anti-tumor activity while avoiding the severe side effects that less selective approaches can cause. Preclinical studies also conducted at CCR indicate that the drug hits its intended marks and stimulates anti-tumor activity in animal models. This new study describes the next step for invika, detailing the results of phase 1 and initial phase 2 experiments in humans.
The researchers leading the trial recruited patients with a wide variety of cancers, the majority of which had not responded well to ICB. In phase 1, they treated study participants with varying dosages of invika every two weeks to evaluate the drug’s safety and determine the optimal dose. While several participants experienced flu-like side effects, these were expected and generally manageable with additional medication and supportive care. After identifying the lowest dose at which desired effects peaked, the researchers advanced to phase 2, treating participants at this optimal dose.
Of the 27 participants treated with the optimal dose across both phases, disease did not progress in 16 (59.3%) of them. Four (14.8%) participants experienced greater than 30% decreases in the size of targeted tumors, two of whom had metastatic colorectal cancer with tumors of a notoriously treatment-resistant type and were receiving invika as their seventh-line therapy. Another responsive participant had stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer, again with tumors that had repelled multiple therapies including ICB. In participants receiving non-optimal levels, invika did not appear to have significant benefit.
In these patients, the study authors found that the drug fostered growth in the target T-cell populations without affecting any other T cells. They linked the four instances of tumor reduction to the largest shifts in target populations, though, as the authors expected at this early stage, immune activity alone did not always produce a measurable clinical response.
“These results are early, and although signs of immune activity don't always translate into benefit to patients at this stage, it is new and exciting to see activity in patients whose cancers had stopped responding to immunotherapy — a group of people with very few options left,” said co-first author Nicholas Tschernia, M.D., a physician-scientist early investigator in the CCR at NCI. “These findings give us a reason to keep studying this new type of immunotherapy, particularly by combining it with other cancer treatments to continue to seek improved results.”
The treatment sponsor, Marengo Therapeutics, previously announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a Fast Track designation to invika to accelerate its evaluation as a treatment for antigen-rich, metastatic colorectal cancer. More recently, FDA has granted the same designation to invika for similar solid tumors, regardless of tissue type, following prior therapy including checkpoint inhibitors.
The ongoing clinical trial is still seeking study participants. Patients interested in enrolling in this study may contact NCI’s toll-free number 1-800-4-Cancer (1-800-422-6237) (TTY: 1-800-332-8615) or email [email protected]. More information can also be found at https://www.cancer.gov/research/participate/clinical-trials-search.
About the National Cancer Institute (NCI): NCI leads the National Cancer Program and NIH’s efforts to dramatically reduce the prevalence of cancer and improve the lives of cancer patients and their families, through research into prevention and cancer biology, the development of new interventions, and the training and mentoring of new researchers. NCI’s intramural research program at the Center for Cancer Research (CCR) conducts innovative, transdisciplinary basic, translational, and clinical studies, including research at the NIH Clinical Center — the world’s largest research hospital. Learn more about the intramural research done in NCI’s CCR. For more information about cancer, please visit the NCI website at www.cancer.gov or call NCI’s contact center, the Cancer Information Service, at 1-800-4-CANCER (1-800-422-6237).
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®

candidato.titulo: Giant, prehistoric rodent fossils discovered in southern Thailand
candidato.resumo: An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, has discovered "remarkably large" rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern Thailand. The finding, published in Scientific Reports, provides a new perspective on the early manifestation of rodent gigantism—the process by which animals evolve to become larger—demonstrating that the evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents is considerably older and more geographically widespread than previously recognized, the researchers said.

texto_fonte:
Giant, prehistoric rodent fossils discovered in southern Thailand
An international team of paleontologists, including researchers from McGill University, has discovered "remarkably large" rodent fossils in the pit of a mine in southern Thailand. The finding, published in Scientific Reports, provides a new perspective on the early manifestation of rodent gigantism—the process by which animals evolve to become larger—demonstrating that the evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents is considerably older and more geographically widespread than previously recognized, the researchers said.
The new species, Yakamys sirindhornae, lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the mid-Paleogene period. The researchers discovered fossils of its teeth—specifically, the lower second molar and lower incisor—at the Bang Mark Pit of the Krabi lignite mine in Krabi Province.
"Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," said Virginie Millien, study co-author and professor of biology at McGill University. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents."
The new genus name, Yakamys, combines the Thai word "yak," meaning giant, with the Greek "mys," meaning mouse or rat.
"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien said.
A rodent far larger than its contemporaries
The fossils were discovered as part of a collaborative research project on fossil mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project involves researchers from McGill University, the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand and French research institutions, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.
Using seven established approaches for calculating body mass from dental dimensions, the researchers estimate that the Yakamys weighed approximately 30 kilograms (66 pounds)—about twice the size of other known rodents from this era, such as the Hulgana.
"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien said.
Because the fossil material is limited, the researchers also noted that it is difficult to determine exactly how the Yakamys evolved. Further discoveries will be important for understanding the animal's biology, ecology and evolutionary history, they said.
Publication details
Yaowalak Chaimanee et al., A giant eocene ischyromyid from Southeast Asia reveals the early evolution of rodent gigantism, Scientific Reports (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-76711-6

candidato.titulo: Robots recognize the shape of an arena by messaging each other
candidato.resumo: Humans can create loose maps of environments they are exploring in their minds, using their senses and navigation skills. Many robots, on the other hand, rely on set maps of known environments or new maps produced using data collected by their sensors.

texto_fonte:
Robots recognize the shape of an arena by messaging each other
Ingrid Fadelli
Author
Humans can create loose maps of environments they are exploring in their minds, using their senses and navigation skills. Many robots, on the other hand, rely on set maps of known environments or new maps produced using data collected by their sensors.
Researchers at Sorbonne University's Institute of Intelligent Systems and Robotics (ISIR), the University of Tokyo and other institutions recently introduced a framework that could allow a swarm of tiny robots to recognize the shape of an enclosure they are in without a map. Their approach, outlined in a paper published in Science Robotics, allows robots to identify the enclosure from a set of known shapes by repeatedly exchanging messages with nearby robots.
"The project addressed a fundamental question in swarm robotics: how can a group of simple robots perceive something that none of its members can observe alone?" Leo Cazenille, first author of the paper, told Tech Xplore.
"It is not unlike the parable of the blind men and the elephant: each man touches only one part of the animal, so none can guess its overall shape. Similarly, each robot can only perceive its immediate neighbors and has no GPS, camera or sufficient memory or computing power to build a map. So how could they recognize the shape of the space they are in?"
Local messages as clues to an enclosure's shape
The recent project originated from a close research collaboration between roboticists, biophysicists and mathematicians. The authors drew inspiration from a famous question posed by the mathematician Mark Kac: Can one hear the shape of a drum?
"The notes a drum produces depend on the shape of its membrane, and we wondered whether a swarm could similarly 'listen' to how numerical information (not sounds) was exchanged between its members," said Cazenille. "The objective was for every robot to learn the shape of the space the swarm occupies without knowing its own position, building a map or relying on a central computer."
The researchers' newly developed approach, spectral swarm robotics, allows groups of robots to learn information about the space they occupy simply by sharing information with their neighboring robots. The term "spectral" comes from the mathematical field of spectral analysis. In this context, it is used to describe the mathematical signature (i.e., spectrum) of an arena's shape.
"The idea is to use the swarm's communication network as a collective sensor," explained Cazenille. "Each robot holds a number representing a virtual temperature and exchanges it with nearby robots, updating its value as though heat were spreading through the group.
"The rate at which temperature differences fade depends on the network of connections, reflecting the geometry of the space occupied by the swarm. By monitoring how its own value changes, each robot can estimate a numerical signature of that geometry and compare it with references for known shapes."
The method proposed by Cazenille and his colleagues only relies on the exchange of short messages between robots and simple calculations. It thus eliminates the need for cameras, information about the position of robots on a map or a central computer that processes the data exchanged by robots.
Tests with real robots
The researchers first assessed their approach mathematically and ran simulations with swarms of up to several hundred robots across seven arena shapes. They also performed experiments with swarms of two different robot types, called Kilobots and Pogobots.
In the real-world experiments, both swarm types successfully used messages exchanged between nearby robots to distinguish a disk-shaped arena from a ring-shaped one. The Kilobots identified the correct shape of an arena in 22 of 30 trials.
"A group of just 25 Pogobots, on the other hand, correctly distinguished between a disk-shaped and a ring-shaped arena in all 30 trials," said Cazenille. "We also identified a relationship between swarm size, communication range and arena area that helps to determine optimal conditions for this method."
Recognizing shapes without a map
Cazenille and his colleagues introduced a new strategy that could allow swarms of robots to infer the shape of their surroundings. This approach could be particularly advantageous for improving the navigation of robot swarms with limited capabilities.
"We demonstrate how the pattern of connections between robots can itself become a tool for sensing and computation," said Cazenille. "Although the presented algorithm focused on identifying the shape of the arena, the approach may be general enough to be applied to more complex tasks involving the local estimation of global properties."
Notably, the team's study focused on the ability of robots to recognize an arena's shape. The extent to which recognizing the shape could improve the swarm's navigation could be assessed in future studies.
The researchers now plan to run experiments with various robot swarms navigating a broader range of environments. They would also like to improve their approach, allowing it to extract richer geometric information about an arena by estimating multiple spectral values.
"Another important development would be to enable robots to keep moving while estimating these properties, so that the method can operate as their communication network changes," added Cazenille.
"We also intend to explore tasks beyond shape recognition, such as identifying boundaries or cavities. In the longer term, our aim is to connect collective perception to action, enabling a swarm to adjust its distribution or formation in response to its perceived environment."

texto_fonte:
Qual é o problema de usar um app desatualizado por muito tempo?
Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Com dezenas de apps instalados no celular, é comum esquecer de atualizar algum deles. Isso não é um problema a curto prazo, mas manter um aplicativo desatualizado por muito tempo pode impedir que a ferramenta funcione corretamente.
Os apps recebem novas versões no Android e iOS para otimizar a experiência e trazer novos recursos. Ainda que algumas soluções sejam atualizadas em segundo plano, é comum que os serviços pouco acessados fiquem defasados.
Por que você deve manter os apps atualizados
A seguir, o Canaltech explica o que acontece ao deixar um app sem atualizações por muito tempo:
App não carrega
Em alguns casos, o aplicativo simplesmente não carrega ou não passa da tela de login. A impressão inicial pode ser de algum erro ou instabilidade e nem sempre o software informa que há uma atualização pendente.
De qualquer forma, ao identificar dificuldade para entrar numa plataforma, vale abrir a App Store ou a Google Play Store para confirmar se não há uma versão mais nova disponível.
Falta de novos recursos
Baixar um novo update ajuda a liberar o acesso a novas ferramentas em apps. As desenvolvedoras podem publicar novidades pelo servidor (sem a necessidade de intervenção do usuário) ou por novas versões nas lojas de aplicativos.
A situação se torna mais crítica quando o recurso é crucial para a plataforma funcionar — nesse caso, a versão desatualizada pode deixar de cumprir tarefas básicas.
Brechas de segurança
Atualizações menores não são menos importante: é comum que os pacotes venham com correções de bugs e ajustes de segurança. Portanto, usar uma versão anterior pode deixar o celular vulnerável a ameaças cibernéticas.

candidato.titulo: Elon Musk signs petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
candidato.resumo: An online petition with over 91,000 signatures is calling for the reinstatement of Nvidia's disgraced former CEO.

texto_fonte:
A letter demanding the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has been circulating online and has already garnered more than 91,000 signatures at the time of writing. Elon Musk said on X that he signed a petition, but it is unclear which one he has signed. At least one large online petition has circulated, with other big names supposedly among the signatories, ostensibly including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and several prominent shareholders, partners, and current and former Nvidia employees. However, the signatories on this petition apparently aren't verified. Regardless, this petition has gathered over 130,000 signatures.
However, not everyone is keen on bringing Jensen back; Nvidia Vice President for Applied Deep Learning Bryan Catanzaro said on X that an online letter purportedly circulated at Nvidia is fake, and he had no involvement and wouldn’t sign it if it were real. He also reiterated his support for Colette Kress, the newly appointed interim CEO who would run the company while the board looked for a suitable replacement for Jensen.
Jensen Huang’s fall was sudden and dramatic — he went from being one of the leading figures in the hardware needed to run AI to completely resigning from the company he built in under two weeks. It all started when U.S. intelligence sources claimed that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apparently close to the former CEO, was passing information to Chinese intelligence. The company initially denied this story, saying, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
But a little over a week after that story, more news came out alleging that Jensen had an affair with the Megaspeed executive, forcing him to finally admit his relationship with the alleged spy. This led to a flurry of investigations by his own company’s board, the U.S. Congress, and the FBI. Just as things were already escalating, another alleged affair surfaced — this time with an Nvidia executive. Amid this whirlwind of scandals and rumors that Jensen would be ousted from the company, Elon Musk said it would be an honor to hire Jensen. Nvidia announced Jensen’s resignation just hours after Musk made the X post.
When do you start your Black Friday shopping?
Despite the nature of his departure, it seems that there is still widespread support for Jensen from Nvidia’s employees, with thousands reportedly rallying behind him and calling for his reinstatement in an internal forum. The Stand with Jensen petition isn’t directly related to Nvidia, but it echoes comments from people inside the company that the former CEO was removed without meaningful due process. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership,” the public letter said. “The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”
Jensen Huang’s larger-than-life persona will be difficult to replace, with the board considering candidates including Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple Chief Hardware Officer Johny Srouji. It’s probably harder for interim CEO Colette Kress, who’s temporarily stepping into the position while the company is in the midst of massive turmoil, especially with the allegations that Huang was removed because of the mass smuggling of up to 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs, and who has the job of reporting its third-quarter results as CEO for the first time on November 17.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

candidato.titulo: New observations challenge evidence for an 'outsize' black hole in the early universe
candidato.resumo: A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 could be a low-mass, metal-poor, star-forming galaxy.

texto_fonte:
New observations challenge evidence for an 'outsize' black hole in the early universe
Shreejaya Karantha
Author
A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity. The paper, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Oct. 14, suggests UHZ1 could be a low-mass, metal-poor, star-forming galaxy.
An early-universe mammoth
UHZ1 was first spotted in the deep NIRCam imaging of the James Webb Space Telescope. Later, astronomers estimated that the galaxy was seen when the universe was around 480 million years old, at a redshift of 10. Using the Chandra X-ray telescope, researchers saw a small excess of high-energy X-rays coming from the spot. They interpreted this signal as a black hole feeding on gas, making UHZ1 an active galactic nucleus (AGN). Some features also hinted at the black hole being buried in thick gas.
They estimated it weighed 10 million to 100 million solar masses, comparable to the mass of all stars in the whole galaxy. This scenario was consistent with the idea of a "heavy seed" black hole that formed directly from collapsing gas—a direct collapse black hole (DCBH), rather than growing slowly from a small star remnant.
This interpretation was somewhat shaky, as it heavily depended on certain assumptions. The JWST's spectrum showed no sign of a black hole, which they thought could be because of heavy dust blocking the emission. The key diagnostic features were outside the instrument's wavelength range, so this could not be tested at the time. "Independent confirmation was therefore urgently needed," the new team writes in the paper.
Chandra and Webb join hands
In their work, the team reprocessed all the old Chandra data along with 0.95 million seconds of new observations. They also analyzed new mid-infrared data from JWST that extend the wavelength range.
The elaborate reanalysis revealed a weaker X-ray detection, and the findings changed depending on the choice of alignment of the X-ray image with the JWST image. They simulated many plausible alignments, and only 0.1% of them gave a signal as strong as the original claim. When they added 0.95 million seconds of new Chandra data, a real and stable X-ray source should have gotten brighter with more observing time. Instead, the new data added almost nothing.
Using these JWST data, the team looked for the kind of emission expected when a powerful black hole buried in dust heats the dust. The mid-infrared instrument (MIRI) did not find any glow of that type. A non-detection does not prove that nothing is there, but it sets an upper limit for the glow. Anything brighter than MIRI's detection limit would have been seen.
Using two templates for what a hidden black hole's light looks like, they scaled each one up until it just reached that limit. That gave a maximum possible brightness for any hidden black hole. But that maximum turned out to be 10 to 1,000 times lower than the original X-ray claim required. So, a black hole as powerful as originally proposed was ruled out.
Escape routes
Next, they checked whether a black hole could still be hiding. There were two ways its infrared glow might be too faint for MIRI to see. First, if the gas had no dust, there would be no glow, in which case the black hole's visible and ultraviolet light would shine through, but that was not seen in JWST data. Second, if the dust were far away and cold, it would glow only in the far-infrared, but ALMA found very little dust, and the galaxy's light was barely dimmed. Neither scenario fit the data, so a luminous hidden "outsize" black hole is very unlikely.
"Our principal conclusion is that no compelling evidence for such an AGN exists," the team notes. Instead, the emission lines are consistent with UHZ1 being a metal-poor, star-forming galaxy of stellar mass around 100 million solar masses, and no black hole is required to explain them.
The team says that since the original claim was extraordinary, they need even stronger proof to support it. In their view, the evidence for a luminous, buried black hole does not meet that bar, as the newly reported X-ray signal is far less significant than first claimed. The infrared data also rule out a black hole as powerful as proposed.

candidato.titulo: Europe’s Digital Wallets May Be More Traceable Than Intended
candidato.resumo: Millions of European Union citizens should soon have access to digital wallets , as member states roll out their implementations of the European Digital Identity Regulation ahead of an end of the year deadline. But the digital identity wallets, which are intended to provide a secure and private place to store identifying information such as bank account information, diplomas, and government IDs such as driver’s licenses, could leave behind a trail of cryptographic clues that makes it possible to recognize someone across services. Cryptographers warn that the technology protecting individual privacy may not yet go far enough to stop people from being tracked. Advances in cryptographic techniques since the law was passed in 2024 means this problem could be solved. However, the law doesn’t require that these techniques be used, and cryptographers that IEEE Spectrum spoke with are split as to whether the wallets should be rolled out at all without such a requirement in place, and whether they’ll be secure enough without it. texto_fonte:
Millions of European Union citizens should soon have access to digital wallets, as member states roll out their implementations of the European Digital Identity Regulation ahead of an end of the year deadline. But the digital identity wallets, which are intended to provide a secure and private place to store identifying information such as bank account information, diplomas, and government IDs such as driver’s licenses, could leave behind a trail of cryptographic clues that makes it possible to recognize someone across services. Cryptographers warn that the technology protecting individual privacy may not yet go far enough to stop people from being tracked.
Advances in cryptographic techniques since the law was passed in 2024 means this problem could be solved. However, the law doesn’t require that these techniques be used, and cryptographers that IEEE Spectrum spoke with are split as to whether the wallets should be rolled out at all without such a requirement in place, and whether they’ll be secure enough without it.
With digital wallets, when someone is asked to provide their ID, a digital, verifiable form of the ID can be transmitted, via a QR code for example. When scanned with a verification app, it would show basic identifying user information, according to Anna Lysyanskaya, a professor of computer science at Brown University.
The EU’s digital identity regulation already includes a requirement for selective disclosure, which allows people to share only the attributes requested by the person checking identification rather than handing over an entire document. A bar checking someone’s age, for example, could request a simple confirmation that a person is over 18 and not need their full name or address..
Tracking Risks in EU Digital Wallets
When the person who requested the ID scans it, they still record some personal information, such as the digital signature and identifiers that are required to check the ID. This additional information can serve as a way of tracking a user even if the attributes shared are quite common. Two requesters could share this information to show they had interacted with the same person, says Johannes Schönrich, the director at the FIM Research Center for Information Management at the Augsburg Technical University of Applied Sciences in Germany
If two parties can share that information, that would be a problem: EU legislation specifies that the wallets should also be unlinkable, which means that “tracking a user by means of [these] digital attestations should not be possible,” says Schönrich.
One way to address the problem is to issue multiple versions of a user’s credentials, each with different cryptographic information attached, says Lysyanskaya. The wallet could keep track of which certificates have already been used, ensuring that a different one is presented during each interaction.
“If you allow a service provider to say, look, I’m not supporting the Google protocol, I want a traditional verification, you essentially allow the service provider to do a kind of downgrade.” —Jaap-Henk Hoepman, Raadboud University
This approach has limitations. If the issuer—the government department that creates and digitally verifies that the credential is authentic—can identify who a credential was originally issued to, it could potentially help link the different versions back to the same person, according to Lysyanskaya.
“Now anybody you’ve ever interacted with has some kind of way of tracking you,” she says.
“If this kind of interaction becomes really ubiquitous … then unless we place a tremendous amount of trust in both issuers and verifiers to guard our privacy, we may encounter a situation where everybody knows at all times what everybody else is up to, by just leaving these little digital crumbs of information about yourself.”
Lysyanskaya was one of sixteen cryptographers who were invited to provide feedback for the European Commission when the law was passed in 2024. They recommended using anonymous credentials, which use zero-knowledge proofs to let people demonstrate their identity or eligibility without revealing unnecessary personal information.
How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Work
Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to convince another that something is true without needing to send any additional information beyond the fact that it is true. For example, they would allow someone to demonstrate that they hold a valid government-issued credential, or meet a particular requirement, without revealing the underlying personal information or creating the same linkable record of the interaction, says Lysyanskaya.
If these two people, the person checking the ID and the person being asked for it ever meet again, there will be no record of any earlier encounters.
The service provider could still verify that the credential is authentic, has not expired or been revoked, and has not been manipulated. However, it would receive less information than it does under traditional verification methods.
“You learn exactly what you need, but not a single bit more about anything that might accidentally be disclosed but is not that necessary,” says Schönrich.
Zero-knowledge proofs have existed in cryptography since the 1980s, but teams of researchers have only recently developed techniques to run them on more constrained devices like smartphones. Shortly after the EU’s digital wallets regulations were passed in 2024, for example, a research team at Google found a way to generate zero-knowledge proofs using credentials signed with the elliptic curve digital signature algorithm, which generates and authenticates digital signatures efficiently enough to be used in a digital wallet.
Those kinds of credentials allow individuals to prove that a credential is valid without revealing the cryptographic signature that could otherwise make separate interactions linkable, according to Jaap-Henk Hoepman, an associate professor of computer science at Radboud University in the Netherlands.
The European Commission wants to conduct more research on implementing zero-knowledge proofs before making them a mandatory requirement for wallet operators from day 1. Because of that, it considers the proofs to be “a core roadmap item,” according to the universal digital blueprint for the wallets. EU governments are free to implement them on a per-country basis if they so choose.
The Commission said on its GitHub page for the wallets that zero-knowledge proofs are not yet mandatory because “there is currently no clear, certifiable approach agreed at EU level,” and that it needs to do more pan-European consultation with cryptographers and groups such as the European Cybersecurity Certification Group (ECCG) that oversee the profession.
“Refinement at this stage focuses on establishing common understanding and boundaries, rather than immediate deployment to secure and privacy-preserving future integration,” their GitHub post from June 2026 reads.
Schönrich says he understands the Commission’s position, but wants them to commit to a binding timeline for introducing zero-knowledge proofs in the next few years for a second version of the wallets.
Karsten Wildberger, Germany’s Federal Minister for Digitalization and State Modernization, unveils the country’s version of the European Union’s EUDI digital wallet in September 2026.Bernd von Jutrczenka/picture alliance/Getty Images
Zero-Knowledge Proofs in EU Digital Wallets
The cryptographers that IEEE Spectrum spoke with are split on whether the EU should ask states to roll out digital wallets without adding in zero-knowledge proofs. The regulation does not specify what type of cryptographic protocols should be used as each country implements its version of the digital wallet, just the privacy requirements.
Hoepman argues that zero-knowledge proofs should be mandated by law so that wallets have to implement this technology. Otherwise, the wallet will not have strong enough privacy protections.
“If you allow a service provider to say, look, I’m not supporting the Google protocol, I want a traditional verification, you essentially allow the service provider to do a kind of downgrade,” Hoepman says. (Some of the cryptographers IEEE Spectrum spoke with advocate for another protocol called the BBS Signature scheme.)
Schönrich believes the EU should proceed with the initial rollout rather than delay the wallets, as even without offering the strongest unlinkability guarantees the wallets are still privacy-friendly. Using lessons from their deployment could also inform a second generation that incorporates the newer cryptographic methods.
However, Hoepman says that online service providers will not want to migrate to a second version because “it will cost them money,” so many will still use the initial version.
Even if a second version becomes available, Lysyanskaya argues that some users may never update their digital wallets unless it becomes mandatory, so the first version needs to be private enough as to not put their IDs at risk.
Hoepman argues that any decision to delay the rollout should be made before the wallets become widely available across Europe. Once businesses and governments have built systems around the first generation, he says, it will be difficult to reverse course.
Anna Desmarais is an award-winning Canadian journalist based in France with a decade of experience writing, filming and broadcasting on both sides of the Atlantic. She covers artificial intelligence, emerging technologies, space, and disinformation. She has reported everywhere from the high Arctic to the hills of Rwanda for outlets including WIRED, Euronews, France 24, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC).

candidato.titulo: Enthusiast builds a working 486 DX2 retro PC on a breadboard in just 16 days, immediately runs Doom
candidato.resumo: An app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486DX2 PC running Doom, put together in just over two weeks.

texto_fonte:
An app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486 DX2 PC running Doom. The intricate explosion-of-wires system build appears to have taken just 16 days, with the first appearance of the legendary Intel CPU on @nagakurage’s timeline on October 24, and a video demo of some fragging in Doom published on November 9. Moreover, the Tokyo-based app engineer behind the project also developed and made a bezelicious ‘CRT monitor’ to go with the homemade early-90s-era gaming beast.
This project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October. On October 24, @nagakurage showcased the legendary Intel i486 DX2 CPU that he had acquired. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.
The enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. We know this is a breadboard PC, but there are limits… Every pin of the 486 CPU appears to have been connected separately to an experimental ‘socket’ made using a baseboard.
A significant milestone was reached on October 26, when the finished form of the breadboard system started to come into view, and the dev managed to get the CPU to blink an LED using x86 code. RAM was added on October 31, and tweaked to be error-free. Then, on November 3, the enthusiast managed to add microSD storage to the system. That same day @nagakurage enjoyed seeing the breadboard 486 boot FreeDOS 1.3 for the first time [machine translation].
The app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.
Finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.
Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

texto_fonte:
Qual é a diferença entre os modelos Muse Wonder, Muse Spark e Muse Ember?
Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
A Meta desenvolveu três modelos de inteligência artificial da família Muse, cada um pensado para um tipo de tarefa. O Muse Wonder é indicado para atividades complexas, que exigem raciocínio e planejamento, e o Muse Spark atende às interações do dia a dia com a assistente Meta AI. Já o Muse Ember foi criado para executar tarefas repetitivas com rapidez e baixo custo.
Os três modelos fazem parte do trabalho do Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL), divisão da empresa dedicada ao desenvolvimento de IA avançada. Embora pertençam à mesma família, eles têm capacidades e recursos diferentes, o que também muda a forma de usar cada um.
Qual é a diferença entre o Muse Wonder, Muse Spark e Muse Ember?
A principal diferença entre os três modelos está no tipo de atividade que cada um consegue realizar. O Muse Wonder é o mais avançado da família e atende a tarefas complexas, como programação, análise de documentos e trabalhos que exigem autonomia por longos períodos. O Muse Spark é mais compacto e rápido, com suporte a textos, imagens, vídeos e áudio. Ele funciona como base da assistente Meta AI nos aplicativos da empresa e nos óculos inteligentes Ray-Ban Meta e Oakley Meta.
Já o Muse Ember prioriza velocidade e economia. Ele foi desenvolvido para executar tarefas repetitivas em grande volume, como leitura de arquivos, extração de dados, chamadas de ferramentas e pequenas operações de programação. A Meta também oferece o Muse Wonder Full, uma versão mais avançada do Wonder, indicada para trabalhos de maior complexidade, que demandam mais capacidade de processamento e raciocínio.
Os modelos também podem trabalhar em conjunto. Nesse cenário, o Muse Wonder fica responsável pelo planejamento e pelas tarefas mais complexas, mas pode delegar parte da execução ao Muse Ember, que cuida de operações menores e repetitivas.
Quais são os recursos de cada modelo?
Veja os recursos de cada um dos modelos:
Muse Wonder
O Muse Wonder é o modelo de maior capacidade da família Muse. Desenvolvido no centro de dados Prometheus, da Meta, ele foi projetado para tarefas que envolvem raciocínio avançado, interpretação de informações e execução de atividades por períodos prolongados. A linha também conta com uma versão mais avançada, chamada Muse Wonder Full, destinada a trabalhos de maior complexidade.
Entre os principais recursos do Wonder estão a Memória Ativa, que recupera informações relevantes de conversas anteriores, e o Foco Ativo, que acompanha objetivos complexos, testa caminhos alternativos diante de erros e solicita esclarecimentos antes de realizar ações importantes.
O modelo também trabalha com projetos extensos de programação, faz alterações em vários arquivos e verifica o funcionamento do código. Ele também consegue interagir de forma autônoma com navegadores, aplicativos para computador e dispositivos móveis. Na área de conhecimento especializado, apresenta desempenho em Direito, Finanças e Saúde, com aplicações que incluem análise de contratos, relatórios financeiros e informações médicas.
O Wonder foi disponibilizado pela Meta Model API e pelo Muse Code, ambiente de desenvolvimento com inteligência artificial. A Meta também prepara o modelo para integrar recursos avançados do aplicativo Muse.
Muse Spark
O Muse Spark foi o primeiro modelo apresentado pela Meta dentro da família Muse. Ele foi desenvolvido para oferecer respostas rápidas e interpretar diferentes tipos de conteúdo, como textos, imagens, vídeos e áudios. É a base da assistente Meta AI no WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, Messenger e Threads, além de estar presente nos óculos inteligentes Ray-Ban Meta e Oakley Meta.
Um dos principais recursos é a visão multimodal, que interpreta imagens, vídeos e informações captadas pela câmera em tempo real. Você pode, por exemplo, apontar a câmera para uma prateleira de alimentos e pedir ajuda para identificar os produtos com maior teor de proteína. O modelo também entende comandos de voz e mantém conversas naturais, com interrupções, mudanças de assunto e troca de idioma.
O Spark ainda conta com o Modo Pensamento, que aciona vários subagentes em paralelo para resolver questões complexas. Em uma pesquisa de viagem, por exemplo, um agente pode procurar hotéis, enquanto outros buscam atrações e opções de transporte.
Nas compras, o modelo apresenta produtos do Facebook Marketplace e de lojas virtuais em um mapa interativo, com filtros de distância, estilo e preço. As recomendações também podem considerar publicações do Instagram, Reels e Threads.
Na área de saúde, o Spark recebeu treinamento com a participação de mais de mil médicos para fornecer informações estruturadas e criar gráficos explicativos. Ele também consegue gerar painéis, minijogos e simuladores a partir de instruções em texto.
Muse Ember
O Muse Ember é o modelo mais leve e econômico da família Muse. Ele foi desenvolvido a partir do treinamento com o Muse Wonder Full e foi criado para cuidar de tarefas menores e repetitivas, principalmente em sistemas que utilizam vários agentes de inteligência artificial. A proposta é deixar os modelos mais avançados responsáveis pelo planejamento, e o Ember encarregado das operações do dia a dia, com rapidez e menor custo.
O modelo consegue realizar a leitura de documentos, extração de informações, organização de dados e pequenas tarefas de programação. Também analisa grandes volumes de arquivos de uma só vez, incluindo projetos de código e documentos extensos.
O Ember ainda interpreta textos, imagens, áudios e vídeos. Com isso, consegue analisar capturas de tela, gravações de reuniões e documentos digitalizados, por exemplo. Sua janela de contexto chega a 1 milhão de tokens, com suporte a respostas de até 512 mil tokens. Essa capacidade ajuda o modelo a processar projetos inteiros de programação e documentos longos em uma única solicitação.
O preço também é um dos diferenciais do Ember. Na API da Meta, o modelo custa a partir de US$ 0,10 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 0,50 por milhão de tokens de saída. A proposta é oferecer uma alternativa econômica para operações em grande volume, com desempenho adequado a tarefas que não precisam dos modelos mais avançados da família.

candidato.titulo: Hybrids make gains in US auto market amid high gasoline prices
candidato.resumo: Electric vehicle growth has hit a speed bump in the United States, but hybrid autos are gaining market share thanks to the jump in fuel prices due to the Iran war.

texto_fonte:
Hybrids make gains in US auto market amid high gasoline prices
Electric vehicle growth has hit a speed bump in the United States, but hybrid autos are gaining market share thanks to the jump in fuel prices due to the Iran war.
Rising popularity of hybrids—which can run on either gasoline or an electric charge—has been a source of U.S. sales increases for Japanese and South Korean carmakers in 2026, prompting fresh investments from both established and new players in that segment of the market.
Honda, a longtime rival to U.S. hybrid market leader Toyota, announced a $3 billion investment this week to build a new hybrid plant in Ohio and add capacity at plants in two other states.
Nissan, which is launching its first significant hybrid product for the U.S. market this fall, realized its absence in the category was denting sales, said Ponz Pandikuthira, a senior vice president at Nissan Americas.
"We were losing that traffic," Pandikuthira said, adding that many customers want to at least explore and test-drive a hybrid even if they end up buying an internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle.
General Motors, which avoided the category earlier in the 2020s when it invested heavily in electric vehicles, plans hybrids "in multiple segments, the key segments that we participate," CEO Mary Barra said last month on a conference call.
"We'll talk more about them as we get closer to the launch," Barra said in response to a question from a Wall Street analyst on an earnings call.
Hybrid electric vehicle volumes have risen by more than a fifth since the middle of 2025, resulting in market share of 16.3% at the end of the second quarter, according to Cox Automotive, an auto services and technology provider.
That's a record and up from 13% a year earlier. The increase stood in contrast with declines in the share of ICE vehicles and EVs, with the latter suffering from the elimination of U.S. tax credits under legislation signed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Gasoline prices have been above $4 a gallon for much of 2026 due to the Middle East war. Prices currently average $3.87 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association.
More options
Nissan's U.S. campaign in the category will begin with the Rogue, a hybrid version of the compact SUV that has been the Japanese automaker's top-selling ICE product in the United States.
Nissan has introduced two generations of hybrid vehicles in other markets, but began working a few years ago on a version better suited to U.S. driving conditions.
"When we use the system in Japan and in Europe, they're mostly in urban driving conditions, which just shines because you're doing stop-and-go traffic," Pandikuthira said.
The new Rogue being unveiled is "optimized for U.S. driving conditions, so that's why it's a home run with climbing, with lots of use on the highway," Pandikuthira said.
The vehicle's other selling point is Nissan's vehicle architecture in which the electric powertrain exclusively drives the wheels, meaning the gasoline-powered engine is only a source of electrons but doesn't actually propel the vehicle.
That system, which Nissan markets as "e-POWER," is designed for a quieter, smoother ride than other hybrid models that drive on a gasoline-fueled engine.
In going with the Rogue, Nissan is picking the most popular vehicle segment for hybrids in the U.S. market. Led by the Toyota RAV4 and the Honda CR-V, compact SUVs account for about 30% of U.S. hybrid sales, said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox.
Valdez Streaty attributes the growth in hybrids not only to higher gasoline prices, but also to greater vehicle choice on the market following product introductions from more recent hybrid entrants including South Korean brands Kia and Hyundai.
She predicted that additional hybrids in popular vehicle classes like pickup trucks or full-size SUVs could sell well.
"It definitely has room to grow," Valdez Streaty said of hybrids' market share.

candidato.titulo: R$ 34 bilhões: Binance cobriu prejuízo do maior roubo de cripto da história
candidato.resumo: Corretora de criptomoedas anunciou aos clientes que cobriu os ativos que foram roubados em ataque hacker no final de outubro. R$ 34 bilhões: Binance cobriu prejuízo do maior roubo de cripto da história

texto_fonte:
Resumo IA
- A Binance anunciou ter cobriu 100% do prejuízo de R$ 34 bilhões decorrente de um ataque hacker no dia 29 de outubro.
- A cobertura foi feita com recursos do fundo de emergência, compra de novos tokens e outras fontes.
- A empresa afirmou que não repassará as perdas para os clientes, mas não informou se recuperou alguma parte dos ativos roubados.
A corretora Binance disse que cobriu 100% dos US$ 6,3 bilhões (R$ 34 bilhões, em conversão direta) que haviam sido roubados no ataque hacker de 29 de outubro. A empresa anunciou a normalização em um post no X. Além disso, também foi publicada uma nova Prova de Reserva indicando a reposição dos criptoativos nas carteiras dos clientes afetados.
Apesar da cobertura integral do roubo, a reposição não significa recuperação: os bilhões de dólares roubados em criptomoedas ainda não voltaram para a empresa. Segundo o site Quartz, a Binance combinou recursos do seu fundo de emergência com a compra de novos tokens e outras fontes para chegar aos 100% do valor roubado.
Esse pode ter sido o maior roubo a criptoativos já registrado. A maior parte do montante foi transferida em apenas 20 minutos. Segundo investigação feita pela TRM Labs, empresa de inteligência em blockchain e cripto, os responsáveis fazem parte do grupo TraderTraitor, supostamente ligado ao governo da Coréia do Norte. O país nega qualquer relação com o ataque.
Operação de guerra para repor os ativos
Uma parte relevante do recurso roubado foi reposta dois dias após as transações fraudulentas. A Binance anunciou em 31 de outubro que havia combinado diferentes fundos para chegar ao montante de US$ 6 bilhões. Entre as fontes estão o seu fundo de emergência SAFU, seu fundo de garantia e também a partir de sua tesouraria corporativa.
Nas últimas semanas, a empresa conseguiu os últimos 10% por meio da compra de tokens, tanto na bolsa de cripto quanto via OTC (over-the-counter, ou mercado de balcão), em negociação direta.
Desde que a situação foi divulgada, a Binance assumiu todos os custos. Até o momento, a empresa não revelou se conseguiu recuperar alguma parte das ações roubadas, mas garantiu que não iria repassar as perdas para os clientes.
Como aconteceu o ataque hacker?
O roubo teria sido realizado por meio do acesso indevido ao computador de um engenheiro de DevOps (setor de desenvolvimento e operações). Uma vez com as credenciais da vítima, os cibercriminosos fizeram diversas transferências autorizadas internamente, sem a necessidade de burlar a segurança para enviar as ações. Segundo a Binance, essa não foi a única vulnerabilidade no caso, e a solução imediata foi bloquear todas as movimentações pela plataforma. O sistema só foi retomado no dia 3 de novembro.
Segundo relatório da TRM Labs, os hackers transformaram um pool de liquidez em uma rota de lavagem de dinheiro. Basicamente, esses ativos foram transferidos e trocados por criptomoedas recém cunhadas pelos próprios criminosos. O valor foi convertido em dólares e, depois, reconvertidos em cripto, utilizando moedas como Ethereum (ETH) e Bitcoins (BTC).
